_: The last resort for style: asking.
Reach for this only when there is nothing to read — no site, no Figma, no
existing code. That is rare, and it should be rare: a client's live site is
the design decisions they have already made and already shipped, and reading
it produces values while asking produces adjectives. `style-from-site` first,
These are forks, not preferences. Each one changes what gets built, has a
default that is defensible when nobody has an opinion, and is recorded as a
decision the moment it is answered — after which it outranks any later
measurement, the same as any other entry in decisions.json.
Keep the list this short. A questionnaire long enough to be thorough is long
enough that the answers stop being considered.

density.question: How much does a screen hold?

options.dense: Operational tools where the user lives all day: more on screen, smaller type, tighter spacing.
options.comfortable: The default. Room to read, one subject per region.
options.spacious: Marketing surfaces and low-frequency tasks: generous whitespace, larger type.

density.changes: the spacing scale's base step, control heights, and the type scale's body size

tone.question: How does the product speak?

options.plain: Says what happened. The default, and the only one that survives translation intact.
options.warm: First person, contractions, a little encouragement in empty states.
options.formal: Full sentences, no contractions; regulated and enterprise contexts often require it.

tone.changes: microcopy, empty states, error messages, button labels
affects: copy rules in the agent contract

colour-commitment.question: How far does brand colour reach into the interface?

options.accent-only: Brand appears on the primary action and little else. The default: it survives a rebrand and keeps contrast easy.
options.branded-surfaces: Brand colour on headers, navigation and large surfaces. Distinctive, and it makes every contrast pair a decision.
options.full-palette: The brand palette drives the whole semantic tier, including status colours.

colour-commitment.changes: how many semantic tokens map to brand stops, and how much contrast work the theme needs

motion.question: How much movement?

options.minimal: State changes and nothing else. The default; it is also the cheapest to keep accessible.
options.expressive: Transitions on entry, layout and emphasis.
options.none: No motion beyond what the platform does. Some regulated and low-power contexts require it.

motion.changes: the duration scale and whether components ship transitions at all
motion.note: Whatever is chosen, prefers-reduced-motion is honoured. That is not a fork; it is WCAG 2.3.3.

theme.question: Which themes ship?

options.light-only: One theme. Half the contrast work, and no theme parity to maintain.
options.light-and-dark: The default for anything people use for hours.
options.system-plus-override: Follows the operating system with an explicit control. The most work, and the most expected.

theme.changes: whether the semantic tier needs a second value everywhere, and doubles the contrast matrix

direction.question: Does the product ship a right-to-left language?

options.rtl-from-day-one: The default when any RTL language is in scope, because retrofitting RTL never finishes.

direction.changes: logical properties become mandatory rather than preferable, and every layout is mirrored in review

component-source.question: Where do the components come from?

options.existing-library: MUI, Ant or similar: a profile already exists or costs a day, and the API is not ours to change.
options.headless-plus-own-styling: Radix, Ark or similar: behaviour and accessibility are solved, appearance is entirely ours.
options.built-from-scratch: Full control, full cost. Only worth it when the product's interaction is genuinely unusual.

component-source.changes: everything downstream: the profile, the bindings, what a screen spec can name
